title: Time Complexity Classes
description: Learn the most common time complexity classes and understand how they affect algorithm performance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Not all algorithms grow at the same rate as input size increases.

Some algorithms remain efficient even with very large datasets, while others quickly become slow and impractical.

Time complexity classes help programmers categorize algorithm efficiency based on how workload increases.

sections.title: Constant Complexity — O(1)
sections.content:
An algorithm with constant complexity performs the same amount of work regardless of input size.

Even if the dataset becomes extremely large, the execution time remains nearly unchanged.

Accessing a specific array element by index is a common example of constant-time behavior.

sections.title: Linear Complexity — O(n)
sections.content:
Linear complexity means the workload grows proportionally with the input size.

If the amount of data doubles, the algorithm generally performs twice as much work.

Scanning through a list one-by-one is a common example of linear complexity.

sections.title: Logarithmic Complexity — O(log n)
sections.content:
Logarithmic algorithms reduce the problem size repeatedly during execution.

Instead of examining every item individually, the algorithm continuously narrows the search space.

This type of complexity is extremely efficient for large datasets and is commonly seen in binary search algorithms.

sections.title: Quadratic Complexity — O(n²)
sections.content:
Quadratic complexity occurs when algorithms use nested iterations.

As the dataset grows, the amount of work increases very rapidly.

Simple sorting algorithms such as Bubble Sort often demonstrate quadratic complexity because every element may need to be compared repeatedly.

sections.title: Comparing Growth Rates
sections.content:
Small differences in complexity become extremely important when working with large datasets.

An efficient algorithm may process millions of items quickly, while an inefficient algorithm may become unusable.

Understanding complexity classes helps programmers choose the right algorithm for different situations.

sections.title: Lesson Summary
sections.content: Time complexity classes describe how algorithm workload changes as input size increases. Common complexity classes include O(1), O(n), O(log n), and O(n²). Understanding these patterns helps programmers analyze performance and design efficient algorithms.
